summary: The School Freedom Act of 2026 terminates existing Federal elementary and secondary education programs by June 30, 2027, and stops new Federal appropriations for them. Instead, it creates 'School Freedom Accounts' managed by the Treasury Department. Eligible children receive federal funds in these accounts, which parents can use either to pay for various K-12 educational expenses—such as private school tuition, homeschooling materials, and tutoring—or direct to their child's public school. Additional funds are provided for children with disabilities, and accounts can accept parental and state deposits with specific tax exemptions. When a student finishes high school, their account converts into a Higher Education and Skills Obtainment Fund for postsecondary expenses until age 30, after which remaining federal funds are returned to the Treasury.

affected_groups.effect: Eligible elementary and secondary students receive School Freedom Accounts containing federal funds that can be used for public, private, religious, or home education expenses, which later convert to postsecondary funds.

Parents decide whether their child attends public school (directing funds there) or use account funds for alternative educational expenses, can make pre-tax contributions or payroll deductions, and face penalties for unauthorized withdrawals.
Receive an additional $2,000 for their first school year in SFAs, adjusted annually for inflation, along with eligibility for specialized educational therapies and assistive technology.
Lose direct federal funding from terminated programs, but receive disbursements if parents choose to allocate SFA funds to public schools or if default allocations apply.
affected_groups.group: Local Educational Agencies and Public Schools

affected_groups.effect: The Department of Education ends covered programs and reorganizes, while the Treasury Department establishes accounts, issues regulations, tracks funds, and collects returned money.

key_provisions: Terminates all covered Federal elementary and secondary education programs no later than June 30, 2027, and halts any new appropriations for them.
Establishes School Freedom Accounts (SFAs) funded by per-pupil federal expenditures, plus extra annual funding for children with disabilities.

Allows parents to use SFA funds for a broad range of qualified educational expenses (including private tuition, books, tutoring, and special needs therapies) or direct the funds to their child's public school.
Permits parents and states to deposit additional funds into SFAs, and provides tax deductions and exclusions for parent and employer contributions.

Converts SFAs into Higher Education and Skills Obtainment Funds (HESOFs) when an individual finishes secondary school or ages out, allowing funds to be used for postsecondary education or career and technical education until age 30.
Imposes tax penalties and potential imprisonment for distributions from SFAs or HESOFs that are not used for qualified expenses.
Directs the Government Accountability Office (GAO) and the Treasury Department to track and report on funding data, account usage, and program implementation.
missing_information: The exact total dollar amount of federal funds that will be appropriated for the School Freedom Account program.
The exact number of eligible individuals nationwide, which determines the per-pupil federal expenditure amount.
summary_detail.plain_summary: The School Freedom Act of 2026 terminates existing Federal elementary and secondary education programs by June 30, 2027, and stops new Federal appropriations for them. Instead, it creates 'School Freedom Accounts' managed by the Treasury Department. Eligible children receive federal funds in these accounts, which parents can use either to pay for various K-12 educational expenses—such as private school tuition, homeschooling materials, and tutoring—or direct to their child's public school. summary_detail.significance: This bill proposes a fundamental restructuring of federal education policy by eliminating traditional federal K-12 education programs and redirecting those funds into individual parent-controlled savings accounts for educational choice. It significantly impacts federal spending administration, shifts educational funding mechanisms toward private and alternative learning options, and introduces new tax rules and penalties for account usage.
